claims.text: The coating consists of alternating nanoscale FCC and BCC high-entropy-alloy layers.
The initial FCC/BCC interfaces are well-defined and coherent.
The as-deposited multilayer has minimal pre-existing dislocation density.
Progressive plastic deformation under sustained loading is governed primarily by evolving interface-mediated dislocation networks.
Severe lattice distortion contributes to the formation of interface-mediated dislocation networks.
Dislocation nucleation is heterogeneous and occurs primarily at FCC/BCC interfaces.
Lattice mismatch at FCC/BCC interfaces facilitates dislocation nucleation and accumulation.
Short-range order at FCC/BCC interfaces facilitates dislocation nucleation and accumulation.
Compositional complexity in the high-entropy layers promotes heterogeneous dislocation nucleation.
Under sustained loading, nucleated dislocations accumulate and interact with interface defects.
Dislocation accumulation and interaction with interface defects cause strain localization and progressive plastic deformation.
Relative to the as-deposited state, sustained loading will increase interfacial dislocation density in the high-entropy-alloy multilayer.
Relative to the as-deposited state, sustained loading will produce localized strain accumulation in the high-entropy-alloy multilayer.
Under identical creep conditions, conventional metallic multilayers will deform more uniformly than the high-entropy-alloy multilayers.
Under identical creep conditions, conventional metallic multilayers will develop less interfacial dislocation buildup than the high-entropy-alloy multilayers.
The proposed mechanism applies when stress and temperature activate creep without causing catastrophic failure or complete interface breakdown.
At sufficiently low stress, creep may not be activated.
At excessively high stress or temperature, alternative failure modes may dominate.

A side-by-side creep test of architecturally similar high-entropy-alloy and conventional multilayers can expose differences in interfacial dislocation evolution, strain localization, creep rate, and deformation morphology.

Failure to observe a significantly larger increase in interfacial dislocation density and localized strain in the high-entropy-alloy multilayer than in the conventional multilayer would falsify the hypothesis.
